title: A deep dive into Biobot’s approach to normalizing viral abundance data
summary: By: Maxim Imakaev, PhD, and Josh Harrison, PhD

# A deep dive into Biobot’s approach to normalizing viral abundance data


Sep 01, 2026


By: Maxim Imakaev, PhD, and Josh Harrison, PhD


*Summary: we have found that normalization cannot rely on pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV) or flow alone to be effective. We have derived a combined ‘hybrid’ normalization metric that uses PMMoV, laboratory efficiency, and flow, allowing us to more precisely compare pathogen abundances across time and space.*


### 1. What is normalization and why does it matter?


Wastewater monitoring provides a fantastic opportunity to understand community health: it is cost-effective, sensitive, inclusive, and non-invasive. However, there are a few key factors that must be considered for wastewater data to be reliable. This is where normalization comes in. Normalization allows us to account for:


1.


**Dilution.** Samples can be diluted by rain or industrial discharge, or any other process that changes sewage flow in a way that is disconnected from how many people flush the toilet. If dilution is not accounted for, then viral abundances will be underestimated.


2.


**Lab process efficiency (“recovery”).** Extraction loss, PCR inhibition, matrix effects—all the things that go bump in the night in the lab. If a laboratory process, say extraction, varies in its outputs, that must be accounted for; otherwise the data become noisy.


Thus,


**normalization allows one to compare wastewater data in time and space** . Consequently, Biobot has put a lot of thought into how to do normalization right.


### 2. What options do we have for normalizing?


There are two main approaches to normalization:


-


**Biomarker normalization:** this approach relies on a marker that ubiquitously occurs in sewage and that is proportional to human contribution. So if more people contribute to the sewage stream, the marker goes up. If the sewage is diluted, it dilutes both the target pathogen and the biomarker equally. The beauty of biomarker normalization is that one measurement can capture both dilution and changes in laboratory recovery. The standard for wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is biomarker normalization.


-


**Flow/population × recovery efficiency:** flow/population handles dilution, and recovery efficiency captures laboratory process variation. Flow/population normalization without the recovery component is frequently used in the WBE literature, even though it


**ignores lab process efficiency** and misses an opportunity to reduce noise in the data.


To normalize data, one divides viral abundance estimates by the normalization factor for biomarker normalization or multiplies them by flow and then divides by population (at Biobot we refer to normalized abundances as ‘effective concentration’).


We use an ‘all of the above’ approach because each style of normalization has its pros and cons.


### 3. So, peppers as a normalizer? Really? Why PMMoV alone is not enough


The WBE community has examined numerous biomarkers as possible normalizers. The de facto favorite is the pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV). This virus infects peppers and, since we humans like tasty food, PMMoV shows up reliably in the waste stream. The thought is that, in aggregate, people consume roughly the same quantity of peppers, and thus PMMoV, over time and space.


PMMoV is a good biomarker on paper: it is highly abundant in human stool, it doesn’t replicate after ingestion, it is diluted in the same way as other targets in wastewater, and it passes through the same lab processes as pathogen targets (i.e. it is a virus, so it functions similarly to other viruses in the lab). All these reasons are why we normalized using PMMoV alone for many years; indeed, it is still the default normalization approach for WBE.


The problem is that PMMoV is not stationary in time.


#### 3.1 PMMoV abundance has changed over time


Biobot and several other large labs contributing to the National Wastewater Surveillance System (NWSS) all show a


**2–3× decline in PMMoV from 2022 to 2024** , followed by roughly 2.5 years of relative stability. Within our own data, PMMoV dropped ~3-fold over the eight months from 2023-07 to 2024-03. This is a problem if PMMoV is the only normalizer used. A 3× drift in the normalization denominator


*is* a 3× drift in reported abundances that has nothing to do with a change in infection rates.


The fact that the same trajectory can be found in public data from independent labs is important: it means that this pattern is not Biobot-specific. It points to something funky going on with peppers. (As a side note, Biobot is one of the few organizations with a dataset spanning enough time and space to observe this pattern.)


**Figure 1.** PMMoV in wastewater declined from 2022 to 2024. National weekly median of samples from wastewater treatment plants serving >10,000 people. Source: Biobot data.


We have also observed multiple shorter-term changes in PMMoV, some rather substantial and only occurring over the period of a few months (see the middle of 2025 in Fig. 1 for an example). Peppers seem to have sickness outbreaks, just like humans, or perhaps these short-term swings are lab artifacts. Either way, we don’t want odd swings in PMMoV to influence normalization.


#### 3.2 PMMoV captures regional differences in water use


We have observed that:


-


**The West has higher PMMoV than other regions.** We have seen this in both Biobot data and other public data.


-


This regional difference


**disappears once we account for the differences in flow.** The West has higher PMMoV because it has lower flow per person (less rainwater inflow, less groundwater infiltration, more water conservation).


This is an example of PMMoV doing its job as intended, correctly capturing regional differences in water use.


#### 3.3 PMMoV does not reduce variability


A good normalization should correct for dilution, reduce lab-based dips/spikes, and make the timelines more smooth on average. However, we observe that on average


**PMMoV normalization does not reduce variability** . While PMMoV normalizes for the relatively rare dilution events or samples with low lab recovery, it also introduces its own variability into the data for all samples. The two are of the same magnitude for our data. The net effect of PMMoV normalization strongly depends on the lab—in publicly available NWSS data from other labs, normalizing by PMMoV often “hurts”. It leads to increased variability compared to no normalization at all.


This does not mean that PMMoV cannot be used as a normalizer. There are methods that would preserve the good effects of PMMoV while reducing the noise it adds to the data. Below we describe how we target PMMoV to account for dilution specifically, and how we combine PMMoV with other normalizers to reduce noise.


#### 3.4 Neither PMMoV nor flow account for dilution perfectly


When we analyzed 21 recent (2025+) flow outliers (defined as flow ≥ 2.5× the mean of the adjacent samples; think big rainstorms), we found that PMMoV concentration does not always follow flow, but neither does SARS-CoV-2.


-


**Ideal behavior:** PMMoV abundance should dip proportionally with flow. So PMMoV × flow would stay flat through a rainstorm. In other words, if there is a lot more flow, we should see a lower concentration of PMMoV because of dilution.


-


**What we observed:** PMMoV × flow frequently spikes


*with* flow. So does SARS-CoV-2 x flow, but to a lesser extent.


This effect has been described in the recent literature (Mercier, 2024). Not all fecal solids deposited in the sewer reach the wastewater plant immediately, some solids precipitate during the normal flow days. PMMoV and viruses precipitate with the solid, but typical viruses slowly leave the solid fraction over the course of several days and are degraded or carried away by the liquid sewage. However, PMMoV stays in the solid fraction for much longer. A high flow event, caused by rain or snowmelt, resuspends the fecal particles, causing a spike in PMMoV load. It also causes a spike in viral load (e.g.


SARS-CoV-2


), but to a lesser extent, since many viruses would have likely left the precipitated solid fraction by then.


In this framework, PMMoV would over-normalize during rain events, while flow would under-normalize. The ideal normalization is likely somewhere in the middle.


#### 3.5 Alternative biomarkers are not obviously better than PMMoV


-


**FSP:** We have found that the F+ coliphage (FSP) correlates only weakly with PMMoV. It tended to be less variable than PMMoV overall but had


*more* outliers in our study. Week-to-week variability showed no discernible difference between FSP- and PMMoV-normalized values.


-


**Endemic-virus panels:** A geometric mean over 5–6 endemic viruses would be inherently low-noise, since we would be combining many independent time series, but individual candidates carry their own seasonality. Also, measuring multiple viruses at once can be burdensome and expensive.


Realistically, we cannot expect one normalizer to do everything.


### 4. We are not the only ones reporting issues with PMMoV


The published record supports both the drift/seasonality and the geographic-structure concerns we note above. Here are some examples:


**PMMoV varies geographically.** Rosengart et al. (2025) modeled two years of WastewaterSCAN data across US treatment plants and found the largest share of PMMoV variance attributable to longitude and latitude, followed by site-membership indicator variables


*i.e.* between-site variability is pronounced. The authors also note one study reporting little seasonal trend and another reporting mild seasonality, and that even within a single person, PMMoV shedding varies substantially over time!


Here are a few other studies to consider:


-


**Denmark, 852 samples / 29 WWTPs / ~49% of national population:** PMMoV had the


*lowest day-to-day* variability of the three markers tested, but a


*pronounced seasonal increase in summer* (Gallagher et al. 2026).


-


**Ontario, Canada (Jan 2021 – Feb 2023, three sewersheds):** PMMoV peaked in January and April 2022 with summer troughs. Flow showed a similar seasonal shape but was


*uncorrelated* or poorly correlated with PMMoV. PMMoV normalization failed to improve correlation with clinical cases at one site and significantly


*reduced* it at the other two (Dhiyebi et al. 2023).


-


**Sweden:** PMMoV was stable over time with no major seasonal or temperature effect, and total PMMoV load was related to population served (Persson et al. 2025).


-


**Kampala, Uganda:** seasonal dilution from rainfall and stormwater infiltration shaped PMMoV concentrations, thus PMMoV was not properly accounting for dilution (Nsawotebba et al. 2026).


-


**A recent multi-site US study (46 studies, 360 sites, 34 states)** concluded PMMoV levels are driven more by sample processing, collection site variation, and population demographics than weather and seasonality (Pappu et al. 2026).


### 5. The PMMoV fix: we remove the changes in PMMoV over time


Since PMMoV abundance drifts over time, we mathematically remove that drift prior to normalization. Briefly, we calculate the per-capita mass of PMMoV in the waste stream as the PMMoV concentration times flow, divided by population. Since this calculation contains flow, it injects the seasonality inherent to flow (e.g. it might rain more in the spring). We then create a smoothed national PMMoV baseline and remove that baseline from each sample. Thus, we omit changes over time due to the pepper ‘epidemic’ but retain the normalizing value of PMMoV. Regional differences are left alone on purpose, because (as we saw above) they reflect real differences in dilution. We refer to this process as ‘deseasoning’. Given that pepper is a common spice, you can consider this a pun.


The math is a bit more complex than what we describe here, and we are planning to write this all up in a more technical publication.


### 6. What about lab recovery and flow?


Rather than choosing between deseasoned PMMoV and flow×recovery for normalization, we blend them together (in log space with fitted exponents). Before anything is blended, each term is clipped to omit outliers, null values are imputed, and the result is then modified through a process we refer to as soft clipping.


#### 6.1 The actual math we chose


normalizer = PMMoV_deseasoned^0.5 · recovery_norm^0.5 / (flow/population)^0.5


The exponents (0.5, −0.5, 0.5) for (PMMoV, flow/population, recovery) mean that we are calculating the


**geometric mean of the PMMoV normalization and the flow×recovery normalization** . We settled on these exponents after doing some optimization to reduce noise in the data, and the fitted values were very close to the chosen geometric mean.


#### 6.2 Soft clipping


A normalizer is only meaningful over the range where it’s actually measuring something. Outside that range, dividing by it doesn’t normalize — it just imposes an offset. So each of the three terms is passed through a smooth sigmoid clamp in log space that behaves like:


-


**In-range:** identity, y = x — normalize normally.


-


**Marginal:** pulled toward the bound.


-


**Far out of range:** fall back toward the


*typical* value of that term, effectively discarding it.


Effects of our soft-clipping approach:


-


The composite normalizer is bounded to roughly


**1.5 orders of magnitude** , versus a very wide window for raw PMMoV. This prevents over-normalization.


-


Composite normalization will not


*cause* extreme effective-concentration outliers - extreme outliers in the normalizers are effectively discarded


-


The overarching benefit is


**reduced location-to-location variability** . This is great for comparing locations.


#### 6.3 Incorporating laboratory recovery


We measure laboratory efficiency by using the bovine coronavirus (BCoV), which is spiked into raw samples before extraction. Each batch has a ‘typical recovery’ that reflects how well the lab was working recently. The value for normalization is in the


*deviations* from typical: the low-recovery outliers identify samples that were inhibited for some reason (extra dirty sewage, perhaps). Consequently, we remove long-term changes in recovery just as we did for PMMoV (using a similar ‘deseasoning’ style approach; this results in the recovery_norm term above).


**Why PMMoV and recovery/flow don’t just duplicate each other.** PMMoV traverses the whole lab process, so in theory it already encodes recovery and dilution. Yet, in practice PMMoV and recovery/flow do not follow the same curve. This discrepancy can be explained e.g. by a non-linear response of PMMoV to extraction variation, or biases in the recovery control. Additionally, PMMoV and flow react differently to rain dilution events (as mentioned above). Taken together, we conclude combining PMMoV, flow, and recovery is safer than just picking one normalization.


Finally, every measurement carries both meaningful signal and noise. Combining multiple measurements together stacks their meaningful effects, but the random noise contributions partially cancel each other out. Statistically, the combination of several normalizers with optimal coefficients would always work better than any individual one. In our case, the optimal coefficients happened to be close to equal contribution for each of the normalizers, which strongly supports using all of the normalizers we have rather than picking the best one.


### 7. To sum it all up


After applying all this math, we found that our hybrid normalization approach reduced week-to-week variation compared to PMMoV alone. Less noise means stronger inferences (Fig. 2).


Fig. 2. Hybrid normalization reduces week-to-week variation relative to PMMoV-only normalization. Absolute fold change between consecutive weekly results at the same site is shown. Medians of boxes are denoted by the horizontal line and median values reported under each box. For all pathogens, hybrid normalization—which used PMMoV, flow, and laboratory recovery—outperformed PMMoV alone.


Hybrid normalization also reduced the number of outliers in the data compared to PMMoV normalization alone.


We have spent years pondering how to extract the most information possible from wastewater. Normalization is complex.


**This new approach clarifies the data and allows us to focus on what really matters: understanding patterns in pathogen abundance in time and space.**
